title: On the Last Mile Problem in Education
author: Rebecca Birch
summary: Rebecca Birch imports the 'last mile problem' from logistics -- the disproportionate cost and complexity of the final delivery step in any network -- as a framework for understanding why promising educational technology consistently underperforms in practice. The article examines three case studies: KhanMigo, quietly cancelled after failing to get students to use it; Alpha School, an iPad-based model achieving impressive gains through highly transactional extrinsic motivation; and coaching programs, which observe teachers but produce little classroom change. Birch argues that the problem is never the quality of the tool but the human motivation gap between possessing access to a resource and choosing to engage with it. The article extends this diagnosis to AI coaching tools entering the market, noting that if human coaches already struggle to bridge the last mile, AI coaches face a steeper barrier still: they cannot apply the social pressure that makes human compliance more likely. Birch closes with a personal analogy from fitness culture -- her actual motivator is her 4:30am training group, not her Apple Watch -- grounding the abstract problem in a concrete truth: the final step of any behavior change requires another person.
points: * KhanMigo was cancelled not because the technology failed but because students would not use it -- in education, 'human motivation is the last mile: the distance from whatever the kid would rather be doing, to sitting in the seat in front of the screen.' * Alpha School's model solves the last mile problem in one narrow sense -- students are extrinsically motivated to finish work quickly to unlock free time -- but at the cost of highly transactional learning that sidelines knowledge-rich curriculum and is largely inaccessible at non-elite price points. * Coaching programs face the same last-mile problem at the teacher level: the observations and conversations happen, but 'having a stagnant coaching program is far more common and is the quiet part that nobody says out loud.' * AI coaching models can provide brilliant feedback at scale, but face a structurally harder last mile than human coaches: they cannot apply the social pressure that makes a coachee comply, making sustained behavior change without human accountability even less likely. * The last mile in education -- from coach to teacher and from teacher to student -- consistently requires a human in the loop; wearable tech and AI tools can support and scaffold, but the actual motivation to cross the final gap is social and relational.
quotes: Khan Academy was a magnet for funding. Given the track record of relative success compared to other edtech endeavours, Khan should have been able to make it work. It seems that the issue wasn't the tool, but the challenge of getting students to use it. In this case, human motivation is the last mile -- the distance from whatever the kid would rather be doing, to sitting in the seat in front of the screen.

Non-human tutors and personalised learning has been around since the 90s. The issue was never, and has never, been the limitations of tech, which has the potential to be as great as the best available human inputs. However, it may be the case that as much as students moan about school, they may actually like their human tutors and socialised learning.

The learning gains are impressive, but the model itself appears highly transactional, in motivation terms. Learning (a race, an obligation) is a chore to be completed in exchange for doing what students really care about. I'm an English teacher, so it's hard for me to imagine how young people might be motivated to learn about war poetry or Shakespeare under this model that seems to sideline a knowledge-rich curriculum.

The problem is common in coaching programs too. The observations happen, the cups of coffee and nice chats happen, but then little change is seen in the classroom. Having a coaching program is a prestige-piece in many schools. Having a stagnant coaching program is far more common and is the quiet part that nobody says out loud.

Several online or AI coaching models are hitting the market, and I can see this being part of our current edtech/AI goldrush. These models can provide brilliant feedback, but again, the challenge is getting the teacher to film, review and act, based on the advice of a non-human coach. The advantage of AI coaching is that these models are potentially scalable in situations where it's difficult and expensive to release teachers from class.

I used to think that concerns about motivation were a bit of a bypass for educators who didn't want to talk about quality teaching and curriculum, or who wanted to shift blame to students when everything was seemingly done right but nothing was really working. I'm not saying by any means that I have solved the problem: it's a wicked one and will only intensify as edtech muscles in on teachers in greater numbers and students increasingly see school as irrelevant and optional.

The last mile in logistics is traversed by a low-paid human in a van from a warehouse in Chullora. And as much as I love my wearable tech, my true motivator is my fitfam, the half-asleep, half-coherent hooligans who get up at 430am most mornings to lift heavy things and put them down again, all to the tune of music I am way too old for. In the same way, the last mile in education is from coach to teacher or teacher to student.
